title: Small-Business Grants
summary: CLASSIFY THE MONEY → CHECK READINESS → APPLY IN ORDER
subtitle: Most small-business grants are not grants. Sorting them out is the entire job.

blocks.text: Most small-business grants are not grants. Some are loans wearing a nicer coat, and one of the five is not money at all.
Sorting the five kinds of money is the entire job. Do it before you fill in a single application.

Small businesses in Canada can get at least five different kinds of money, and almost everyone calls all five a grant. This module sorts out what each one costs you, what a real application needs, and the order that gets you funded instead of stuck.
Knowing which “grant” is a loan keeps your business from signing up for debt it did not plan for.
blocks.detail: Five kinds of money look alike in an ad, and each one costs you something different.
blocks.extra: Section 02 sorts the five kinds of money.

sections.title: Five Kinds of Money, and What Each One Costs You

blocks.text: Every one of these gets called a grant by somebody with an incentive to call it that.

items.title: Non-repayable contributions
list: Real grants. You meet the criteria, do the project, keep the money.
Almost always reimbursed after you spend, so a grant only helps a business that can already afford the project.
Delivered mainly through regional development agencies: ACOA, CED, FedDev, FedNor, PrairiesCan, PacifiCan, CanNor.

items.title: Repayable and conditionally repayable contributions
list: Money for a project that you repay, usually interest-free, often starting once the project is done or revenue hits a threshold.
Conditionally repayable versions are forgiven if set milestones are not met.
Still a liability on your balance sheet from the day you sign.

items.title: Loans and loan guarantees
list: The Canada Small Business Financing Program has the government guarantee part of the loan to the lender, not to you. You owe every dollar, at a market rate.
Futurpreneur pairs financing with two years of mentorship for entrepreneurs under forty.
Targeted loan funds exist for women, Black and Indigenous entrepreneurs. Good loans, but loans.

items.title: Tax credits
list: The quietest, and often the largest. SR&ED reimburses a share of qualifying research and development work.
Claimed on the corporate return, not applied for, which is exactly why they get missed.
Non-refundable ones are worth nothing to a business with no tax payable, which describes most businesses in their first years.

items.title: Advisory and in-kind support
list: Small Business Enterprise Centres, Community Futures offices, Futurpreneur mentors, provincial innovation agencies.
Free or nearly free, undersubscribed, and often the fastest route to the money in the other four categories.

items.title: “There is a big pot of free government money for anyone starting a business.”
items.text: There is a large pot of funding, but most of it must be paid back, is for certain industries or is tied to a set project, not to starting a business in general. Programs also close. The Canada Digital Adoption Program, heavily advertised for years, closed in 2024 and is still cited by consultants. If a page selling you something has no recent date, treat it as fiction.

blocks.text: CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: THE FEE-TAKING GRANT CONSULTANT

A whole industry stands between you and this money. Some of it is honest: experienced grant writers who charge a fair fee for real work on hard applications. Some of it is not. The pattern to watch for is a cold approach by email, phone or social media, promising funding you have never heard of, followed by a fee up front, a cut of any money awarded, or both. Warning signs: they will not name the program before you pay, they claim a link to a government department, they promise approval, or they charge you to learn about programs listed for free on the Business Benefits Finder. Before you pay anyone, look up the program name on the federal Business Benefits Finder and your regional development agency’s site. If the program exists, you can apply yourself or get free help from a Small Business Enterprise Centre or a Community Futures office. If it does not exist, you have your answer. An honest consultant will have no problem with you checking first.

sections.title: You cannot apply for anything without these

blocks.text: Funding applications fail at the paperwork stage far more often than on merit. Gather these once, and every application after that takes a fraction of the time.

items.title: Business number and incorporation or registration documents.
Two years of financial statements, or projections with the assumptions written down if you are pre-revenue.
A defined project with a start date, an end date and a budget, not a general need for money.
Evidence you can fund the project first, since most contributions reimburse after you spend.
Your matching contribution identified, because most programs require you to cover a share.
A named person responsible for reporting after the money arrives.

blocks.text: That fourth item deserves its own sentence. The most common shock in this course is learning that an approved grant does not arrive as a cheque before the work. It arrives as a refund after you have paid the bills, sent the claim and waited. A business that cannot carry the project until then cannot use the grant, no matter how well it applied.

items.title: “I will apply now and figure out the matching contribution later.”
items.text: Your matching share is usually a condition of approval, not a detail after it. Applying without knowing where your share comes from wastes weeks and strains a relationship with a program officer you may want again next year.

sections.title: What a funding agreement does to your balance sheet

blocks.text: CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: WHAT A FUNDING AGREEMENT DOES TO YOUR BALANCE SHEET

Say yes to a contribution you must repay, and three things change at once. None of them appear in the announcement. First, you have taken on a debt, and your lender will see it the next time you apply for credit. Second, most grants you do not repay are taxable to the business or lower the cost base of what they paid for, so part of that money goes back at tax time. Budget for it. Third, government help usually lowers what you can claim for other credits. A wage subsidy on a researcher’s pay lowers the part of that pay you can claim for research credits. None of this makes the funding a bad idea. It makes combining programs a math problem, not a collection. Before you sign, ask the program officer: is this taxable to us, does it reduce any other credit we claim, and when does repayment start? Write the answers down. Program officers hear these questions rarely and answer them gladly.

items.title: Run the Business Benefits Finder first
items.text: It is the federal government’s own questionnaire across many programs. It is free, and it finds programs no consultant needed to tell you about.

items.title: Call your regional agency and your local support office
items.text: Ask what is open this quarter. Fiscal-year budgets get allocated in spring and depleted through the year, so timing beats eloquence.

items.title: Classify every option by instrument
items.text: Grant, repayable contribution, loan, tax credit or advice. Write the label next to each name, so future-you does not have to work it out again.

items.title: Define the project before you shop for money
items.text: Programs fund projects, not ambitions. A dated scope with a budget can go to five programs; a general wish for growth cannot go to any.

items.title: Confirm the reimbursement mechanics and matching requirement in writing
items.text: Then check your cash flow against them before you commit to a supplier.

items.title: Set up the reporting on day one
items.text: Most agreements need progress and money reports, and a missed report can mean paying back money you already got.

sections.title: Sylvie, the cold email, and the eleven hundred dollars

paragraphs: Sylvie runs a bakery in Trois-Rivières with four employees and a fifteen-year-old oven. Lately the oven makes a noise nobody wants to identify. Her goal is to replace it before it dies in the middle of the Christmas rush.

The new oven costs more than the business has. Then an email arrives. A firm offers to find her government money for new equipment. It has a slick website and a logo that sits suspiciously close to a federal wordmark.

The fee is $1,100 up front, plus a cut of anything she gets. They will not name the program before she pays. They say it protects their research. Sylvie has run a business through two recessions and a pandemic. She finds this a slightly odd way to protect anything.
Still, the oven is getting louder. Paying feels faster than searching. Sylvie decides to make one free call first. She phones her local Community Futures office.

In twenty minutes, the counsellor names two programs. One is a regional fund that is partly paid back. The other is a provincial rebate on energy-saving equipment that nobody had mentioned. Sylvie had been thinking about ovens, not power bills.

He also tells her the catch that matters most. The fund pays her back after she buys the oven, so she will need about four months of bridge money. Her credit union covers the gap at a rate that does not frighten anyone.
Sylvie gets the oven before the rush. The funding covers a real share, and the rebate covers more than she expected. The $1,100 stays in the account, which in a bakery is a lot of flour.

blocks.text: Before anything else, sort the money: grant, repayable contribution, loan, tax credit or advice. Use the Business Benefits Finder and call your regional agency yourself before you pay anyone a fee. Define a dated project with a budget, not just a need for money. And confirm in writing whether the money pays you back after you spend, because a grant you cannot carry is a grant you cannot use.
Sylvie found two programs and kept $1,100 by making one free call before paying a consultant.
blocks.detail: Checking the program yourself first can save your own business the fee and find money nobody mentioned.
blocks.extra: Your action this week, in Section 08, starts with the Business Benefits Finder.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): Your Funding Map

items.title: Run the federal Business Benefits Finder, and save the results with today’s date on them.
Book a free appointment with your regional development agency, Small Business Enterprise Centre or Community Futures office. Ask what is open this quarter and when their intake windows fall.
Write your project on one page: what, when, how much, and what changes in the business afterward. That page is the raw material for every application you will file.

blocks.text: One rule of thumb: if you cannot name the instrument, grant, loan, credit or repayable contribution, you are not ready to apply for it yet.

items.title: Non-repayable contribution
items.text: A real grant. Usually paid back to you after you spend, and often taxable to the business.

items.title: Repayable contribution
items.text: Project money you pay back, often with no interest and a delayed start. It is debt, not a grant.

items.title: Conditionally repayable
items.text: You only pay it back if set conditions or sales targets are met.

items.title: Regional development agency
items.text: The federal bodies that give out regional business funding: ACOA, CED, FedDev, FedNor, PrairiesCan, PacifiCan and CanNor.

items.title: Community Futures
items.text: Local non-profit offices that give business advice and loans in rural and small-town Canada.

items.title: Matching contribution
items.text: The share of project cost you must pay yourself. Usually a condition of approval, not a detail.

items.title: SR&ED
items.text: The federal research and development tax credit, claimed on the business tax return, not applied for.

items.title: Business Benefits Finder
items.text: The Government of Canada’s free questionnaire for finding programs. The first stop, and the reason most consultant fees are not needed.

items.title: WHERE TO GET HELP
list: Business Benefits Finder: the official federal tool covering federal, provincial and territorial programs. Free.
Your regional development agency: ACOA, CED, FedDev Ontario, FedNor, PrairiesCan, PacifiCan or CanNor, depending where you are.
Community Futures or SADC offices in rural regions, and Small Business Enterprise Centres in urban ones. Free advice, and they know the current intakes.
Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre: 1-888-495-8501, to report a grant-funding solicitation that misrepresents a government relationship.

blocks.text: This module skips dollar figures on purpose. Program caps, cost-share ratios and intake budgets change every fiscal year, and at least one heavily advertised federal program has closed since 2024. Confirm current terms on the program’s own page.

quiz.question: True or False: “There is a big pot of free government money for anyone starting a business.”

questions: What is your project, in one sentence, with a start date and a total budget?
Which programs did you find, and what kind of money is each one? (Grant / Repayable contribution / Loan / Tax credit / Advice)
How much of the cost must you cover yourself, and where will it come from?
Does the money arrive before you spend, or after? (Before / After / Not sure)
If it arrives after, how will you cover the gap, and about what will that cost?
Has anyone asked you for a fee to find funding? (Yes / No) If yes, have you looked up the program yourself?
